title: Why the Waltons Still Own 45% of Walmart | Mohnish Pabrai at Copenhagen Business School
description:
Mohnish Pabrai's Session with Copenhagen Business School Investment Club on August 25, 2026.

summary: The video argues that investors should prioritize finding exceptional, long-term holdings over the skill of selling, even if their error rate in other investments is high. It highlights Walmart as a prime example of such a holding, noting its ability to offset portfolio losses and its history of compounding returns since 1972. The speaker also discusses other positions like Rayas and Kaspi, emphasizing the importance of holding great businesses indefinitely to allow compounding to work without interruption.
thesis: The video argues that investors should prioritize finding exceptional, long-term holdings over the skill of selling, even if their error rate in other investments is high. It highlights Walmart as a prime example of such a holding, noting its ability to offset portfolio losses and its history of compounding returns since 1972. The speaker also discusses other positions like Rayas and Kaspi, emphasizing the importance of holding great businesses indefinitely to allow compounding to work without interruption.

claims.claim: The speaker highlights Walmart as an exceptional holding that should be held indefinitely without selling, citing the Walton family's long-term ownership and the stock's ability to offset portfolio losses.
claims.quote: The important thing was not to buy Walmart. The important thing was not to touch Walmart, to never sell it, no matter what was happening, no matter what the company said and what they reported, etc. You just kept it.
claims.speaker: Mohnish Pabrai

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the Walton family has never sold Walmart since it went public in 1972 and currently owns more than 46% of the company.
claims.quote: The Walton family, they owned 46% of Walmart when it went public in 1972. And after 54 years, they own more than 46% of Walmart. So the Walton family in 54 years has never sold Walmart.
claims.speaker: Mohnish Pabrai

claims.claim: Walmart delivered about 15 or 16% annualized returns from 1972 to 2026, demonstrating that one exceptional holding can offset losses from other stocks in a portfolio.
claims.quote: And if you looked at the returns from 1972 when Walmart became public to 2026 54 year period including reinvested dividends Walmart has delivered about 15 or 16% a year annualized
claims.speaker: Mohnish Pabrai

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that finding exceptional companies like Walmart is more important than being good at selling, even if one has a high error rate in other investments.
claims.quote: And when we get a trip to the pie counter, we have to load up on a lot of pie and then try not to drop that pie till you get back to your table. And someone asked him once, how can one be good at selling? And his response was, don't worry about becoming good at selling. Worry about becoming good at finding Costos.
claims.speaker: Mohnish Pabrai

claims.claim: The Walton family refused diversification advice and kept their massive stake in Walmart, relying on its dividends and community contributions.
claims.quote: The Walton family told them very politely to off and they just kept their shares. And Walmart gives a dividend. you know the dividend might be like six 7 billion a year 5 to 7 billion a year or something I don't know some kind of dividend like that they end up with 2 three billion a year in dividends it's enough to live on
claims.speaker: Mohnish Pabrai

claims.claim: The Walton family decided they did not need to diversify their holdings despite warnings about concentration risk.
claims.quote: basically, the Walton family decided we don't need to diversify. Now we come to Babry Funds and we have like three stocks in Turkey that make up like 65 or 70% of the funds I manage. And these are not my funds. I have investors. So I tell my investors, dear investors, Monish is not going to sell any of these things. He is not going to diversify.
claims.speaker: Mohnish Pabrai

claims.claim: The speaker notes that the Walton family has held Walmart for 54 years without selling, and advises investors to hold great businesses even if they appear overpriced.
claims.quote: And after 54 years, they own more than 46% of Walmart. So the Walton family in 54 years has never sold Walmart. And because Walmart has bought back shares, they actually own a higher percentage of the company. So they followed that principle of just holding.

claims.claim: The speaker states that Rayas is worth significantly more now due to compounding, with a liquidation value of 3 billion compared to 800 million in 2019, and advises leaving the position alone to avoid interrupting compounding.
claims.quote: So what was a business that was worth 800 million in 2019 is now worth 3 billion. And again, I can do the same math. I go to a broker in Istanbul, show the portfolio, they're going to say, this portfolio is worth like 3.4 billion and there's 400 million of debt. So the market cap is 1.8 billion.

claims.claim: The speaker emphasizes that the founders of Rayas are exceptional capital allocators who only invest if they see returns of 25 to 35% a year in dollars or euros, ensuring the business continues to compound.
claims.quote: Now I made the bet and what I did not realize when I made the bet is that the father and son who ran this business were exceptional capital allocators. They do not invest capital if they do not see a return in dollars or euros and that all their money comes back in two or three years.

claims.claim: The speaker plans to hold the Rayas position for the long term, meeting with founders annually to encourage them to continue running the business for decades.
claims.quote: And so what am I supposed to do with RAS in Turkey? What I'm supposed to do is spend all my time talking to the students at the Copenhagen Business School. Leave the RAS position alone. Like Charlie says, do not interrupt compounding unnecessarily.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Kaspi as an exceptional business with a strong management team, high growth, excellent margins, and a monopoly-like competitive position, trading at a significant discount to comparable Western businesses.
claims.quote: His question is uh one of your most recent investments is Kaspi in Kazakhstan. uh which appears to be an exceptional business with a strong management team, high growth except excellent margins and a monopoly like competitive position.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Kaspi trades at around nine times trailing earnings, which is a significant discount to comparable businesses in the US or Western Europe that trade at around 30 times earnings.
claims.quote: Uh comparable business in the US would or in the western Europe might trade at more like 30 times earning whereas Casp is trading at uh around nine times trailing earnings uh largely reflecting the geographic exposure into Kazakhstan.
